title: Determining the Smallest Worthwhile Effect of Exercise in Patients with Rheumatic Musculoskeletal Diseases A Benefit-Harm Trade-Off Study
summary: Professional societies recommend physical activity and structured exercise for people with rheumatic diseases. However, exercise costs time, effort and sometimes money, and may involve risks. It is not known how much symptoms must improve with exercise before patients feel the effort is worthwhile. Research question: What is the smallest additional improvement in pain, tiredness and limitations in daily life that an exercise programme must achieve for people with rheumatic diseases to consider it worthwhile? Does this differ between one-to-one training with a physiotherapist, training in a group and training with a smartphone app? And which personal characteristics are related to it? Methods: 100 to 150 adults with rheumatic diseases from Austria, Germany and Switzerland complete a single online questionnaire. They read descriptions of the three exercise programmes and indicate step by step the improvement at which each programme would be worthwhile for them. They also answer questions about themselves, their disease, their symptoms and their physical activity. No exercise is delivered as part of the study, and there are no further appointments.
conditions: Rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases (inflammatory rheumatic diseases, including axial spondyloarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren’s disease, sarcoidosis)

interventions.name: Adults with a rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease complete a single electronic questionnaire (REDCap – Research Electronic Data Capture). criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
(1) Physician-diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease OR (2) self-reported diagnosis of a rheumatic disease commonly associated with inflammatory arthritis (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, sarcoidosis, Sjögren’s disease, systemic lupus erythematosus) when recruited via patient organisations; AND (3) age ≥ 18 years, sufficient German language skills to provide consent, willingness to participate.
Exclusion criteria:
No electronic informed consent; no rheumatic diagnosis, or chronic primary pain or osteoarthritis as the only diagnosis.
